doc.title: Howard Mandel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Discovering jazz on Chicago's South Side; piano and flute lessons
summary: Mandel grew up near the Stony Island divide, drawn to Ramsey Lewis, R&B, Miles, Coltrane and Dolphy, thinking of jazz as dramatic and abstract. He had piano and flute lessons.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: You know you and I are actually very close in age, and I think back when I was starting to listen to records and for some reason I was hearing like Little Eva and “The Locomotion.” I’m wondering why you got into jazz, apparently at an early age?

Well I was listening to Ramsey Lewis and “The In Crowd” and rhythm & blues music, it was on the local radio. I grew up in Chicago and I lived in a community that was on the South Side of Chicago so it was a neighborhood that was divided by Stony Island Avenue which is a large commercial street, and on one side was the black neighborhood and on the other side was the white neighborhood, but we went to the same grammar schools. And I just didn’t understand what the distinction was, why there was this kind of divide in the community. And so I was curious about my black neighbors and playmates, schoolmates. And I liked the music from an early age. My parents had a few jazz records, they were not heavy listeners, they mostly listened to show tunes. But I liked, they had some Classical music, and I liked the Russians. I liked the drama. Rimsky-Korsakov, anything with the rhythm and the exotic colorations. And I heard that in some of the jazz music that I was exposed to also. And so I just gravitated to it very naturally. It just seemed like, yes I like instrumental music, I like this kind of rhythm & blues feel with the back beat, I liked it more than the country & western sort of influence that was coming in from Elvis and that level of rock & roll. And I liked the complexity. I was also an intellectual snob at an early age and I thought that the music that I was really interested in early, Miles Davis, some early Coltrane, Eric Dolphy around 1963, ’64, it just seemed to © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

me akin to the movies I was watching, I was exposed to some early Truffaut and Goddard, that sort of thing. And I saw those kinds of connections. So I didn’t really see it as like swing or bebop, I just knew it as dramatic, fractured, abstracted, fast, that sort of thing.
I understand you took some piano.
I had some piano lessons. When I was in high school I took some flute lessons. I still play flutes and a little bit of saxophone. In college I took some synthesizer courses and stuff like that.
